endorsements.quote: Authors should present sufficient data to replicate analyses and enable readers to explore specific strengths and weaknesses of the trialled application(s).
Thus, authors can define the ground truth using various sources, the most important of which are evidence-informed clinical practice guidelines.
An additional example is red teaming, where humans or AI models are used to circumvent model safeguards, which is a more intensive form of stress testing that can help improve model robustness.

Methods might include stress testing or using challenging prompts to simulate real world variation and possible user behaviour and observing whether trialled applications have the adaptability and flexibility to provide useful responses and avoid generating dangerous or harmful content.

unlisted_practices: Authors of chatbot health advice studies should report the name, version identifier, and date of release or last update of the generative AI model and chatbot evaluated.
Authors should state whether evaluated generative AI models and chatbots are open-source or closed-source.
Authors should describe the prompt development process, sources of prompts, and the number and expertise of individuals involved in prompt engineering.
Authors should provide all study prompts and all chatbot outputs or responses, or report their unavailability as a major limitation.
Authors should report the date and location of chatbot queries and whether prompts were entered in separate chat sessions.
Authors should evaluate and report the reproducibility of chatbot responses.
Authors should define the ground truth or reference standard used to judge chatbot performance and describe how responses are classified, preferably a priori in a study protocol.
Evaluators should be masked to chatbot identity where feasible, and authors should state whether blinding was applied.
Authors should report how sample size was determined.
Authors should include patients and members of the public in prompt engineering and performance evaluation where applicable and report their involvement.
Authors should report the nature, frequency, and magnitude of chatbot responses that deviate from the ground truth.
Authors should systematically classify potential harm from chatbot responses, for example with the WHO International Classification for Patient Safety.
Authors should report conflicts of interest and funding sources and their role in the study.
Authors should describe ethical approval or waiver and measures to safeguard patient data privacy.
Developers should move towards open-source generative AI models to enable transparent evaluation.

screen.reason: This is a reporting guideline and explanation/elaboration consensus document (CHART) for studies evaluating AI chatbots in healthcare advice.
